props.title: The Housemaid

sections.content: **The Housemaid** (2010) marks a stunning modernization of Kim Ki-young's 1960 Korean classic, with director Im Sang-soo transforming the original's domestic horror into a sleek commentary on class warfare. Like Park Chan-wook's The Handmaiden (2016) and Bong Joon-ho's Parasite (2019), it dissects Korean social hierarchy through the lens of household dynamics. The film's calculated tension builds through the relationship between a wealthy family and their new maid, echoing similar power dynamics found in **Rebecca** (1940) and **The Piano Teacher** (2001).

sections.content: Im Sang-soo's visual approach creates a stark contrast to the 1960 version, trading expressionist shadows for cold modernist architecture. The pristine mansion becomes a character itself, similar to the oppressive environments in **I Am Love** (2009) and **The Servant** (1963). Jeon Do-yeon's nuanced performance as Eun-yi carries echoes of other complex domestic worker portrayals like those in Roma (2018) and **Diary of a Mad Housewife** (1970).

The film's exploration of power dynamics extends beyond just class commentary into gender politics, particularly relevant in the #MeToo era. Like **Elle** (2016) and **The Piano Teacher** (2001), it subverts expectations about female agency and victimhood. The calculated way the wealthy wife and mother-in-law manipulate situations draws parallels to the methodical social climbing in Burning (2018) and **Sympathy for Lady Vengeance** (2005). sections.content: **The Housemaid** (2010) sits within a broader movement of Korean films examining social inequality through genre elements. While Bong Joon-ho's **Snowpiercer** (2013) uses science fiction and **The Host** (2006) employs monster movie tropes, Im Sang-soo's approach is more intimate but equally devastating. The film's ending, both shocking and inevitable, follows the tradition of Korean social thrillers like **Mother** (2009) and **Thirst** (2009) in refusing easy moral conclusions.
